J U D G M E N T
body: Muhammad Jaffer Raza J. – The Petitioners are importers and manufactures engaged in the automotive industry. Some Petitioners import components, subassemblies and raw material for manufacturing auto parts; some Petitioners Page 8 import components, including components in kit form (“CKD”) for assembly/manufacture of vehicles; whereas some Petitioners also import complete built-up units (“CBU”) of vehicles. The imports relate to vehicles classified under Chapter 87 of the Pakistan Customs Tariff (“PCT”). The Petitioners before us fall within two broad categories, namely; (a) Greenfield Investors; (b) Existing Manufacturers of vehicles and auto-parts.

2. By virtue of the aforesaid petitions, the Petitioners have impugned Additional Customs Duty (“ACD”) levied by the Federal Government under section 18(5) of the Customs Act, 1969, (“Act, 1969”) effected through a series of Statutory Regulatory Orders (“SROs”), on the import of material, components etc. used in the manufacture of vehicles and auto-parts. The impugned SROs, the list whereof, as challenged by both categories of Petitioners cumulatively, are tabulated hereinunder (“Impugned SROs”): - SROs Date Effect SRO 630(I)/2018 24.05.2018 Superseded SRO 1178/2015. ACD levied @ 2%, excluding goods SRO 670(I)/2019 28.06.2019 Superseded SRO 630/2018. ACD levied on tariff slabs @ 2% to 7%, excluding goods imported under SRO 693/2006.

SRO 572(I)/2020 30.06.2020 Superseded SRO 670/2019. New slabs for ACD created, excluding goods SRO 845(I)/2021 30.06.2021 Superseded SRO 572/2020. New slabs for ACD created, excluding goods SRO 967(I)/2022 30.06.2022 Superseded SRO 845/2021. New slabs for ACD created, excluding goods imported under SRO 693/2006. No change in duty for Petitioners.
SRO 929(I)/2024 30.06.2024 Superseded SRO 967/2022, excluding goods imported under SRO 693/2006.
No change in duty for Petitioners.
SRO 1151(I)/2025 30.06.2025 Supersedes SRO 929, excluding goods imported under SRO 693/2006. No change in duty for Petitioners.

3. Prior to recording the submissions advanced by the learned counsels, it will be prudent to briefly elucidate the undisputed background of the present Page 9 challenge. Pursuant to a decision of the Economic Coordination Committee (“ECC”), the Federal Government introduced the Automotive Development Policy 2016-21 (“ADP”) on 21.03.2016. Through the said policy, automobile industry was incentivized to invest in the automotive sector. These commitments were subsequently implemented and given effect through various notifications, SROs and Investment Agreements, details of which shall be elucidated below.

4. For context, it is imperative to note that prior to the introduction of the ADP, the customs duties prevailing in the automotive sector were levied by the following SROs: - (i) SRO 655(I)/2006 dated 22.06.2006.

The noted SRO, under section 19 of the Act,1969 provided partial exemption from customs duty payable under the First Schedule. The exemption was in respect of “raw materials, sub-components, components and sub-assemblies, as are not manufactured locally, imported for the manufacture of components and assemblies as specified in Table-I”. The noted SRO benefitted auto-parts manufacturers.

The noted SRO, under section 19 of the Act,1969 provided partial exemption from customs duty specified in the First Schedule. The exemption was in respect of “components (which include sub-components, components, sub-assemblies and assemblies but exclude consumables), imported in any kit form, and direct materials for assembly or manufacture of vehicles falling under Chapter 87 of the First Schedule”. The noted SRO benefitted assemblers and/or manufacturers of vehicles.

The noted SRO, under section 18(5) of the Act,1969 levied ACD. Clause (a) levied ACD on goods listed in Appendix I, which were components/parts for vehicles. Clause (b) levied ACD on subcomponents and components “imported as part of any kit form for the assembly or manufacturing of” certain types of vehicles. The SRO clarified that: “the additional customs duty shall be levied on the sub-components and components which become indigenized by the New Entrant assembler or manufacturers, in accordance with the said plan for progressive manufacturing.” Page 10 Succintly, components listed in this SRO were those that were required by auto policies to be ‘indigenized’ or ‘localized’ i.e. required to be manufactured in Pakistan. Thus, ACD imposed by this SRO was only on localized components in order to discourage their import and not on ‘nonlocalized’ components.

For clarity, the levy was on the import of all goods specified in the First Schedule @ 1%, but goods imported under SRO 693/2006 were expressly excluded. By implication, goods imported under SRO 656/2006 were subjected to ACD.

5. As noted above, the ADP 2016-2021 was issued on 21.03.2016 with the primary object to lower the entry threshold for new investment in the autosector and to create an enabling tariff structure for development of the automotive sector. To encourage new investment, the ADP introduced investment categories of Greenfield and Brownfield with different incentives.

6. To give effect to the various aspects of the ADP, the Ministry of Industries and Production issued several notifications dated 02.06.2016, all bearing No. 2(9)/2013-LED-II. The two notifications that are germane to these petitions are:

i. SRO 2(9)/2013-LED-II dated 02.06.2016 which provided the “Five Year Tariff Plan of customs duties”, hereinafter “ADP Tariff Notification”; ii. SRO 2(9)/2013-LED-II dated 02.06.2016 which notified the investor categories of Greenfield Investment and Brownfield Investment along with the offered incentives, hereinafter “ADP Investor Notification”.

7. The latter envisaged a “New Entrant Agreement” between the Federal Government and the new investor. Pursuant thereto, the Petitioners who were eligible as Greenfield Investors, entered into Investment Agreements with the Federal Government.

Category A defined “Greenfield Investment” as: - “The installation of new and independent automotive assembly and manufacturing facilities by an investor for the production of vehicles of a make not already being assembled/manufactured in Pakistan.”

For the purpose of clarity, the other category i.e. Category B pertained to “Brownfield Investment”, which is not relevant for the purposes of the instant adjudication as none of the Petitioners fall into the said classification.
Page 11 8. In furtherance of the ADP Tariff Notification and the ADP Investor Notification, the Federal Government issued the following SROs under the Act,1969:

9. The ADP Tariff Notification, the ADP Investor Notification, the Investment Agreements, SROs 482, 483 and 484 of 2016 shall cumulatively be referred to as “ADP Implementing Instruments”. The following paragraphs shall encompass the salient features of the listed SROs.

10. The noted SRO was issued under section 19 of the Act,1969 to amend SRO 655/2006 to provide a partial exemption from customs duty levied under the First Schedule on “raw materials, sub-components, components and sub-assemblies, as are not manufactured locally, imported for the manufacture of components and assemblies as specified in Table-I”. This SRO benefitted auto-parts manufacturers. SRO 483/2016.

11. The noted SRO was also issued under section 19 of the Act,1969 amending SRO 656/2006. Clause (a) of the noted SRO exempted certain components imported in any kit form and direct materials for assembly or manufacture of vehicles mentioned in Table-I, from so much of customs duty as specified in the First Schedule as is in excess of the rates specified in Table-I. Clause (a) of this SRO benefitted Existing Manufacturers of vehicles.

12. Clause (b) of the noted SRO exempted certain goods imported by a Greenfield Investor or Brownfield Investor for assembly or manufacture of certain vehicles, from customs duty specified in the First Schedule as is in excess of the rates specified in Table-II. The goods listed in Table-II were components in kit form, both localized and non-localized. Table-II also specified the duration of the exemption. To illustrate, for passenger cars Page 12 classifiable under PCT heading 87.03, customs duty on CKD non-localized was fixed @ 10% for 5 years for a Greenfield Investor, and 3 years for a Brownfield Investor; whereas customs duty on CKD localized was fixed @ 25% for both investors for 5 and 3 years respectively.

13. Clause (c) of this SRO exempted vehicles in CBU and plant and machinery imported by a Greenfield Investor, from customs duty specified in the First Schedule to the extent mentioned in Table-III. The Explanation clause of the SRO clarified that “non-localized” components were those that were not listed in the Appendices to SRO 693/2006, whereas localized component were those that were listed in SRO 693/2006.

14. The noted SRO was issued under section 18(5) of the Act,1969 to amend SRO 693/2006 whereby ACD had been previously levied. Clause (a) of the SRO reduced ACD on goods listed in Appendix I, which were components/parts for vehicles. Clause (b) changed the rate of ACD on components specified in the Table, imported as part of any kit form for assembly or manufacture of vehicles mentioned in the Table.

15. As noted for SRO 693/2006 supra, the ACD levied under the noted SRO was only on localized components. For this reason, the components or sub-assemblies imported by auto-parts manufacturers under SRO 482/2016 were not affected because that exemption was available only if components were not manufactured locally.

16. What is relevant for the purpose of present adjudication is that the levy of ACD through the noted SRO included the following proviso: - “Provided further that in line with Auto Development Policy (ADP) 2016-21 the 18th March, 2016 notified by Ministry of Industries and Production vide Notification No. 2(9)/2013-LED-II dated 2nd June, 2016, the additional customs-duty leviable under this notification shall not be charged on sub-components and components, imported in any kit form, by an assembler or manufacturer declared to be an investor under Category-A “Greenfield Investment” for a period of five years and under Category-B “Brownfield Investment” for a period of three years, for Page 13 assembly or manufacturing of the vehicles, excluding vehicles at Sr. No. 1, 7, 9, 11 and 12, specified in the above Table”.

17. With the promulgation of SRO 482, 483 and 484 of 2016, the rate of customs duties applicable to the Petitioners are summarised as follows: - (a) for Existing Manufacturers of passenger cars classifiable under PCT heading 87.03: customs duty on CKD under SRO 483/2016 (both on localized and non-localized) became 30%; plus ACD under clause (b) of SRO 484/2016 on any localized component imported as part of a CKD became 16% (total 46%).

(b) for auto-parts manufacturers related to vehicles classifiable under PCT heading 87.03: customs duty under SRO 482/2016 became 1% on raw material, 10% on sub-components and components, and 20% on subassemblies i.e. if those were not manufactured locally.

(c) for Greenfield Investors who manufactured passenger cars classifiable under PCT heading 87.03: customs duty on CKD non-localized under SRO 483/2016 became 10% for 5 years; customs duty on CKD localized under SRO 483/2016 became 25% for 5 years; there was no ACD as per the proviso to SRO 484/2016.

18. It is also imperative to highlight that SRO 656/2006 was further amended by SRO 837/2021 dated 30.06.2021. The amendment stipulated inter alia that 30.06.2026 would be the expiry date of concessions given to new investors under the ADP as follows:

“xiva) The concessionary custom duty for various models of new entrants under ADP 2016-21 to continue for five years from date of first manufacturing certificate of respective variant issued by Engineering Development Board or upto 30th June 2026, whichever is earlier;”
19. It is undisputed that the effect of the Impugned SROs was to increase the rate of ACD beyond the rate stipulated in SRO 484/2016, as noted above.

20. Succinctly stated, the case of the Petitioners is that the imposition of ACD through the Impugned SROs was in violation of the commitments made by the Federal Government in the ADP Implementing Instruments. Page 14 21. On behalf of the Petitioners, arguments were led by M/s. Ali Hussain Almani and Khalid Javed Khan Advocates. Learned counsel representing other Petitioners adopted the same, with M/s. Qazi Umair Ali and Nadeem Qureshi Advocates making additional submissions. For the Respondents, arguments were led by Mr. Zahid F. Ebrahim, learned counsel representing the FBR, with M/s. Agha Shahid Majeed Khan, Syed Ahsan Ali Shah and Khalid Rajpar Advocates for the customs department making additional submissions. The learned DAG representing the Federal Government adopted those submissions.

22. Mr. Ali Almani, learned counsel for Petitioners, submitted that the ADP issued by the Federal Government made a commitment to both Existing Manufacturers and new investors such as Greenfield Investors, that the rate of customs duties would remain unchanged for 5 years. Such commitment, according to the learned counsel, was also reflected in the Investment Agreements between the Federal Government and Greenfield Investors. He further contended that the words “customs duties” used in the ADP Tariff Notification signified that ACD too would not be increased in the prescribed/protected period and upon such commitment, the Petitioners made investments in the auto industry and acquired a vested right in those instruments for the said period, which rights cannot be abridged and are protected by the doctrine of promissory estoppel. Reliance was also placed on Section 6 of the Protection of Economic Reforms Act, 1992 (“Act,1992”).
